imo-1985-01.title: Tangent lengths and a half-angle identity
imo-1985-01.body:
Let $O$ be the centre and $r$ the radius, and write $A,B,C,D$ also for the angles of the quadrilateral. Since the circle is tangent to lines $AD$, $DC$, $CB$, the point $O$ is at distance $r$ from each of them. $O$ lies on side $AB$ and $O\ne A,B$ (its distance $r>0$ from line $AD$ and from line $BC$ is positive), so $O$ is inside the angles $ADC$ and $BCD$ of the convex quadrilateral; being equidistant from their sides, $O$ lies on their internal bisectors: $\angle ODA=\frac D2$, $\angle OCB=\frac C2$.

**Side $AD$.** Let $T$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to line $AD$, so $OT=r$. Measuring signed lengths along line $AD$ in the direction from $A$ to $D$: from the right triangle $OAT$ with $\angle OAD=A$ we get $AO=\frac{r}{\sin A}$ and the signed length $AT=AO\cos A=r\cot A$ (negative if $A$ is obtuse). From the right triangle $ODT$, $TD=DO\cos\frac D2=r\cot\frac D2$. Hence
$$AD=AT+TD=r\cot A+r\cot\tfrac D2 .$$
In the same way $BO=\frac{r}{\sin B}$ and $BC=r\cot B+r\cot\frac C2$.

**Use the circle $ABCD$.** Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to $180^\circ$: $D=180^\circ-B$ and $C=180^\circ-A$. So $\cot\frac D2=\cot(90^\circ-\frac B2)=\tan\frac B2$ and $\cot\frac C2=\tan\frac A2$. Therefore
$$AD+BC=r\Big(\cot A+\tan\tfrac A2\Big)+r\Big(\cot B+\tan\tfrac B2\Big).$$

**Identity.** For $0<x<180^\circ$,
$$\cot x+\tan\tfrac x2=\frac{\cos x\cos\frac x2+\sin x\sin\frac x2}{\sin x\cos\frac x2}=\frac{\cos(x-\frac x2)}{\sin x\cos\frac x2}=\frac1{\sin x}.$$

Hence $AD+BC=\dfrac{r}{\sin A}+\dfrac{r}{\sin B}=AO+OB=AB$, because $O$ lies on segment $AB$. ∎

imo-1985-02.title: Walk through the multiples of $k$
imo-1985-02.body:
Write $i\sim j$ if $i$ and $j$ have the same colour. For $j=1,2,\dots,n-1$ let $r_j\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ be the remainder of $jk$ modulo $n$. Since $\gcd(k,n)=1$, these remainders are distinct and nonzero, so $\{r_1,\dots,r_{n-1}\}=M$. Also $r_1=k$. It suffices to show $r_j\sim r_{j+1}$ for $1\le j\le n-2$.

We have $r_{j+1}\equiv r_j+k\pmod n$, and $r_j+k\ne n$ because $r_{j+1}\neq 0$.

**Case $r_j+k<n$.** Then $r_{j+1}=r_j+k>k$, so $r_{j+1}\ne k$, and rule (ii) with $i=r_{j+1}$ gives $r_{j+1}\sim |r_{j+1}-k|=r_j$.

**Case $r_j+k>n$.** Then $r_{j+1}=r_j+k-n<k$, so again $r_{j+1}\ne k$, and rule (ii) with $i=r_{j+1}$ gives $r_{j+1}\sim k-r_{j+1}=n-r_j$. By rule (i), $n-r_j\sim r_j$. Hence $r_{j+1}\sim r_j$.

So $r_1\sim r_2\sim\dots\sim r_{n-1}$, and these are all the elements of $M$: all of $M$ has one colour. ∎

imo-1985-03.title: Induction on the largest exponent, using $(1+x)^{2^m}\equiv 1+x^{2^m}$
imo-1985-03.body:
Only parities matter, so we work with polynomials over $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$; then $w(P)$ is the number of nonzero coefficients. Two facts:
- $w(U+V)\le w(U)+w(V)$, so $w(U)\le w(U+V)+w(V)$;
- if $\deg U<N$ and $\deg V<N$, then $w(U+x^NV)=w(U)+w(V)$ (the two parts use disjoint powers of $x$).

Also $(1+x)^{2}\equiv1+x^2$, and by repeated squaring $(1+x)^{2^m}\equiv1+x^{2^m}\pmod 2$.

We prove the statement by strong induction on $i_n$. If $i_n=0$ then $n=1$ and there is nothing to prove. Let $i_n\ge1$ and choose $m\ge0$ with $2^m\le i_n<2^{m+1}$. Put $N=2^m$ and split the exponents into $L=\{i_t: i_t<N\}$ and $H=\{i_t:i_t\ge N\}\ni i_n$. For $i\in H$, $Q_i=(1+x)^N Q_{i-N}\equiv(1+x^N)Q_{i-N}$ with $i-N<N$. So
$$P:=\sum_t Q_{i_t}\equiv R+(1+x^N)S=(R+S)+x^NS,\qquad R=\sum_{i\in L}Q_i,\quad S=\sum_{i\in H}Q_{i-N},$$
where $\deg R<N$ and $\deg S\le i_n-N<N$. Hence $w(P)=w(R+S)+w(S)$.

**Case 1: $L$ is empty**, i.e. $i_1\ge N$. Then $R=0$ and $w(P)=2w(S)$. Now $S$ is a sum of distinct $Q$'s with smallest index $i_1-N$ and largest index $i_n-N<i_n$, so by the induction hypothesis $w(S)\ge w(Q_{i_1-N})$. Moreover $Q_{i_1}\equiv(1+x^N)Q_{i_1-N}=Q_{i_1-N}+x^NQ_{i_1-N}$ with $\deg Q_{i_1-N}<N$, so $w(Q_{i_1})=2w(Q_{i_1-N})$. Thus $w(P)\ge 2w(Q_{i_1-N})=w(Q_{i_1})$.

**Case 2: $L$ is nonempty**, so $i_1\in L$. Then
$$w(P)=w(R+S)+w(S)\ge w(R).$$
$R$ is a sum of distinct $Q$'s with smallest index $i_1$ and all indices $<N\le i_n$, so by the induction hypothesis $w(R)\ge w(Q_{i_1})$. Hence $w(P)\ge w(Q_{i_1})$.

This completes the induction. ∎

imo-1985-04.title: Parity vectors and pigeonhole, twice
imo-1985-04.body:
The primes not exceeding $26$ are $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$ — nine of them. Every element of $M$ is $2^{e_1}3^{e_2}\cdots23^{e_9}$; call $(e_1\bmod2,\dots,e_9\bmod2)$ its *parity vector*. There are $2^9=512$ possible parity vectors. Two numbers with the same parity vector have a product with all exponents even, i.e. a perfect square.

**Step 1: many disjoint pairs with square products.** As long as at least $513$ elements of $M$ remain, two of them have the same parity vector; remove these two as a pair. Starting from $1985$ elements, after $t$ pairs $1985-2t$ elements remain, and we can continue while $1985-2t\ge513$, i.e. for $t=0,1,\dots,736$. So we obtain $737$ disjoint pairs $\{a_j,b_j\}$ with $a_jb_j=c_j^2$, $c_j$ a positive integer ($j=1,\dots,737$).

**Step 2.** Each $c_j$ also has no prime factor larger than $23$. Since $737>512$, two of them, $c_j$ and $c_l$ ($j\ne l$), have the same parity vector, so $c_jc_l=d^2$ for an integer $d$. Then
$$a_jb_ja_lb_l=c_j^2c_l^2=d^4,$$
and $a_j,b_j,a_l,b_l$ are four distinct elements of $M$ because the pairs are disjoint. ∎

imo-1985-05.title: Radical centre and powers of a point
imo-1985-05.body:
Let $\omega$ be the circle with centre $O$ and radius $r$, $\Gamma$ the circumcircle of $ABC$ and $\gamma$ that of $KBN$. Products like $XU\cdot XV$ for collinear $X,U,V$ are signed (positive iff $U,V$ are on the same side of $X$); then the power of $X$ with respect to a circle through $U,V$ equals $XU\cdot XV$. We use directed angles $\angle(\ell,m)$ between lines, modulo $180^\circ$.

**$KN$ is not parallel to $AC$.** Since $A,K,N,C$ are concyclic, $BK\cdot BA=BN\cdot BC$. If also $KN\parallel AC$, then $\frac{BK}{BA}=\frac{BN}{BC}$, and together $BA=BC$; then the homothety with centre $B$ taking $K\mapsto A$ takes $N\mapsto C$ and $\gamma$ to $\Gamma$, so $\gamma$ and $\Gamma$ would be tangent at $B$, contradicting that they meet at two points.

**The radical centre.** Let $P=AC\cap KN$. Line $AC$ is the radical axis of $\omega,\Gamma$, line $KN$ that of $\omega,\gamma$, so $P$ has equal powers with respect to all three circles and lies on the radical axis $BM$ of $\Gamma$ and $\gamma$. Note $P\ne B$ ($B\notin AC$), and $P\notin\Gamma$: $P$ is on line $AC$, and $P=A$ would put $A$ on line $KN$, which meets line $AB$ only at $K\ne A$ (as $N\notin AB$); similarly $P\ne C$. In particular $P\ne M$. The powers of $P$ give
$$PM\cdot PB=PK\cdot PN=PO^2-r^2. \tag{1}$$

**$M,N,C,P$ are concyclic.** Using $P\in BM$, then $\gamma$, then $\omega$, then $P\in CA$:
$$\angle(MN,MP)=\angle(MN,MB)=\angle(KN,KB)=\angle(KN,KA)=\angle(CN,CA)=\angle(CN,CP).$$
$C,N,P$ are not collinear (that would force $P=C$), so $M,N,C,P$ lie on a circle. The power of $B$ with respect to it, and then with respect to $\omega$, gives
$$BM\cdot BP=BN\cdot BC=BK\cdot BA=BO^2-r^2. \tag{2}$$

**Conclusion.** Put coordinates on line $BP$: $B=0$, $P=p\ne0$, $M=m$, and let $F=f$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$, with $OF=d$. Then $BO^2=f^2+d^2$, $PO^2=(p-f)^2+d^2$, $BM\cdot BP=mp$ and $PM\cdot PB=(m-p)(0-p)=p(p-m)$. Subtracting (1) from (2):
$$mp-p(p-m)=BO^2-PO^2=f^2-(p-f)^2\iff 2mp-p^2=2pf-p^2\iff m=f.$$
So $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to line $BM$, i.e. $\angle OMB=90^\circ$. ∎

imo-1985-06.title: Nested intervals and expanding differences
imo-1985-06.body:
**Reformulation.** If $x_n>0$, then $x_{n+1}>x_n\iff x_n+\frac1n>1\iff x_n>1-\frac1n$. Hence the condition "$0<x_n<x_{n+1}<1$ for every $n$" is equivalent to
$$1-\tfrac1n<x_n<1\quad\text{for every }n\ge1 \tag{$*$}$$
(for $n=1$ this reads $0<x_1<1$; the inequality $x_{n+1}<1$ is ($*$) for $n+1$, and $x_n>0$ follows from ($*$)).

**The $x_n$ as functions of $x_1$.** Write $x_n=P_n(x_1)$. Then $P_1(t)=t$ and $P_{n+1}=P_n\,(P_n+\frac1n)$, so by induction each $P_n$ is a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients and $P_n(0)=0$; on $[0,\infty)$ it is continuous and strictly increasing (a product of positive increasing functions for $t>0$). Also $P_n(1)\ge1$ by induction ($P_{n+1}(1)\ge 1\cdot(1+\frac1n)$). By the intermediate value theorem there are unique $a_n<b_n$ in $[0,1]$ with $P_n(a_n)=1-\frac1n$ and $P_n(b_n)=1$ (for $n=1$: $a_1=0$, $b_1=1$). Since ($*$) needs $x_1>0$, $x_1$ satisfies ($*$) iff $a_n<x_1<b_n$ for every $n$.

**Existence.** $P_{n+1}(a_n)=(1-\frac1n)\cdot1=1-\frac1n<1-\frac1{n+1}$, so $a_{n+1}>a_n$; and $P_{n+1}(b_n)=1\cdot(1+\frac1n)>1$, so $b_{n+1}<b_n$. Thus $(a_n)$ is strictly increasing, $(b_n)$ strictly decreasing and $a_n<b_n$ for all $n$ (so $a_n<b_m$ for all $n,m$). Let $a=\sup a_n\le b=\inf b_n$. Then $a_n<a\le b<b_n$ for every $n$, so $x_1=a$ works.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $y_1<z_1$ both satisfy ($*$) and let $d_n=z_n-y_n$. Then $d_1>0$ and
$$d_{n+1}=z_n^2-y_n^2+\tfrac1n(z_n-y_n)=d_n\Big(z_n+y_n+\tfrac1n\Big).$$
By induction $d_n>0$, and for $n\ge2$, by ($*$), $z_n+y_n+\frac1n>2(1-\frac1n)+\frac1n=2-\frac1n\ge\frac32$. Hence $d_n\ge(\frac32)^{n-2}d_2\to\infty$, contradicting $0<y_n<z_n<1$, i.e. $d_n<1$. So exactly one $x_1$ works. ∎
